analysis.title: Weekly Global: What to watch in the week ahead
key_insights: The S&P 500 gained 1.2% last week and hit a record close on Tuesday. The 10-year Treasury yield eased later in the week after approaching its highest level in nearly 25 years.

September CPI on Wednesday is the main data test. A stronger reading could revive expectations for an October Fed rate increase. PPI and retail sales on Thursday give more evidence on pipeline inflation and consumer strength under higher energy prices.

Bank earnings are a second test of resilience. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report Tuesday, followed by Morgan Stanley and Bank of America on Wednesday. They should show consumer spending, credit quality, capital markets activity and the effect of higher financing costs.

UBS base case is that the Fed can wait until December before another rate increase. Softer employment data, slower wage growth and encouraging underlying inflation reduce the urgency to tighten in October.

UBS expects AI investment, resilient activity and robust earnings growth to support further equity gains. It recommends keeping diversified equity exposure across sectors and regions, and says volatility could persist if inflation surprises up or yields resume their rise.

French 10-year yields approached 5%, close to a 24-year high. The spread over German yields stayed near levels last seen in the Eurozone debt crisis. Italian yields also rose and the Stoxx Europe 600 declined.

France's 2027 budget debate begins in the National Assembly on Tuesday. Markets will watch whether higher French borrowing costs spread to Italian bonds, corporate credit or broader financial conditions. The IMF and World Bank annual meetings and Eurozone industrial production and final September inflation are also due.

UBS does not see an imminent European funding crisis. French issuance still draws solid demand, and higher yields and wider spreads are already tightening financial conditions. It stays Attractive on European fixed income, favoring short- to medium-term maturities and stronger investment grade issuers, and Attractive on Eurozone equities.

Brent ended the week near USD 105 a barrel despite better Gulf crude exports and a G7 agreement to release 100 million barrels from emergency reserves. Attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure continued, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport over the weekend.

UBS raised its year-end Brent forecast by USD 5 to USD 100 a barrel, citing declining inventories and escalating attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. It expects Strait traffic to recover gradually with periodic setbacks and sees risks tilted toward continued energy volatility.
UBS favors diversified broad commodity exposure over a single energy outcome. Industrial metals can benefit from electrification, AI infrastructure and rising power consumption.

Referenced UBS notes: reserve releases may limit near-term oil spikes but will not resolve market tightness, copper faces a widening deficit and higher prices, and high real yields and a firm dollar may weigh on gold near term while structural demand supports the longer-term outlook.
The chart of the week shows the 3-month average of monthly nonfarm payroll change trending softer, which supports the view that the labor market is cooling.

sector_views.rationale: UBS is Attractive on Eurozone equities. Improving revenues, accelerating investment and stronger profit momentum should help absorb moderately higher yields.
UBS is Attractive, with selective opportunities in short- to medium-term maturities and stronger investment grade issuers. It sees no imminent funding crisis.
UBS favors broad commodity exposure as protection against supply shocks, geopolitical stress and inflation spillovers.
Robust profit growth and AI investment are expected to let equities absorb moderately higher rates. UBS advises staying invested near record highs.

earnings_insights: US bank earnings this week (not yet reported): JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo on Tuesday, Morgan Stanley and Bank of America on Wednesday. They are a read on consumers, credit quality and capital markets activity.
UBS expects European Q3 results to be supported by improving revenues, cost discipline, structural investment and more favorable currency effects, despite higher rates and energy costs.

risk_factors: A hotter September CPI could revive October rate hike expectations and push yields up again.
French and Italian fiscal stress could spread to corporate credit and financial conditions.
Renewed attacks on energy infrastructure could reverse the recent progress in oil flows.
Elevated yields and energy costs pressure borrowers, consumers and corporate margins.
charts_described: Chart of the week: 3-month moving average of monthly change in US nonfarm payrolls, seasonally adjusted, shown as trending softer. The text gives no levels.
vol_and_positioning: UBS says equity volatility could persist if inflation surprises to the upside or yields resume their rise.
geopolitical: Attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure in the Gulf continued, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport over the weekend.
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is recovering but unevenly.
A US-backed proposal for an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine is awaiting support from both sides.
G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves.
France's 2027 budget debate begins Tuesday, and the IMF and World Bank annual meetings take place this week.
